title: Build or Buy: What Growing Your Own 310T Actually Costs in 2026
excerpt: Ontario issued 436 Truck and Coach certificates in all of 2025. Ottawa rewrote the apprenticeship funding stack in April, two grants quietly died the year before, and the certification rate is 19.9%. What the numbers say about training versus hiring.
author: Certus Technical Search
content:
Ontario issued 436 Certificates of Qualification in Truck and Coach Technician in all of 2025. Not applications. Not registrations. Finished, certified 310Ts, for the entire province.

That number is why every shop owner eventually asks the same question: should we stop competing for the few and grow our own? In 2026 the answer changed, because Ottawa rewrote the funding stack in April and two grants your bookkeeper may still be budgeting for quietly died the year before.

*Current as of September 2026. The federal programs below are moving; confirm before you file.*

## What is actually claimable today

**Federal Apprenticeship Job Creation Tax Credit.** 10% of eligible wages, to a maximum of $2,000 per apprentice per year, for the first 24 months of a Red Seal program. Claimed on your return.

**Ontario Achievement Incentive.** Up to $17,000 per apprentice, paid to the sponsor: up to $2,000 at registration for youth and under-represented apprentices, $1,000 for each completed in-class level with enhancements available, and $1,000 at certification.

**Ontario Tools Grant.** $1,000 for motive power trades. Worth knowing that motive power draws the highest tier here, against $600 for construction and industrial and $400 for service.

**Ontario Apprenticeship Completion Employer Bonus.** $1,000 taxable, on certification.

**Canada Apprentice Loan.** $4,000 interest-free per technical training period to a $20,000 lifetime maximum, available everywhere except Quebec. Not money to you, but it removes a reason your apprentice walks during in-school.

## What died, and what hasn't opened yet

The **Apprenticeship Incentive Grant** and the **Apprenticeship Completion Grant** both ended 31 March 2025. If either is still in a spreadsheet somewhere in your office, take them out.

In April 2026 the federal government announced **Team Canada Strong**: $6 billion over five years, targeting 80,000 to 100,000 new Red Seal trades workers and an explicit goal of halving time to certification. Inside it sit a $2 billion apprenticeship service offering up to $10,000 toward a first-year apprentice's salary, a $5,000 Red Seal completion bonus, and a training grant of $400 per week during mandatory in-class time, up to $16,000, paid on top of EI.

That last one matters more than it looks. In-school is when apprentices disappear, because for weeks they stop earning shop wages. A grant that pays during those weeks addresses the actual failure point.

The catch: the intake window has been announced, not opened. Plan around the money that exists today and treat Team Canada Strong as upside.

## The number nobody puts in the brochure

The Canadian Apprenticeship Forum surveyed 533 British Columbia employers on their 2022 apprentices and calculated return per dollar invested, by trade:

- Industrial Mechanic (Millwright): **$1.50**
- Heavy Duty Equipment Technician: **$1.41**
- Automotive Service Technician: **$1.32**

Being straight with you: there's no Truck and Transport Mechanic line in that study. HDET and AST are the nearest proxies. But every trade close to this work returned more than it cost, and the industrial trades outperformed construction.

## Then the part that should give you pause

Statistics Canada's 2024 figures, released last December, show a record 101,541 new apprenticeship registrations, up 5.9% and the highest since the series began. Certifications came in at 46,971, up 1.0%, still 9.6% below pre-pandemic levels.

The rates underneath: **19.9% certification. 30.9% discontinuation.** Roughly half are still in progress.

So the honest framing is this. Apprenticeship returns about $1.40 on the dollar for the apprentices who finish, and nearly a third don't. Training is not a fix for a bay you need covered this quarter. A 310T is 6,720 hours, 6,000 on the job and 720 in school across three levels, which is about three and a half years. A 421A is 7,000 hours.

One counter-signal worth knowing, because it complicates the shortage story honestly: heavy duty equipment mechanic certifications rose 41.5% in 2024 and passed 2019 levels. That corner of the trade is recovering faster than the headline suggests.

## The rule that changes who can work Monday

In Ontario, **310T is compulsory. 421A is not.**

To work in Truck and Coach legally, a person needs a Registered Training Agreement, a Provisional Certificate of Qualification, or a Certificate of Qualification, and the certificate has to be kept current. There's no equivalent requirement for Heavy Duty Equipment Technician.

Practically, an uncertified body can work heavy equipment in Ontario and can't work trucks and coaches. Shops get this wrong, and it's not the kind of wrong you want to find out about during an inspection.

Compulsory certification for truck and transport also applies in Nova Scotia and Alberta and is voluntary in the rest. Quebec doesn't use this model at all, training heavy-vehicle mechanics through a school-based 1,800-hour DEP rather than employer-sponsored apprenticeship, so most of the above doesn't apply there.

## How to decide

Build if you have a licensed journeyperson with the patience to teach, work steady enough to carry someone through three levels, and a vacancy you're trying to prevent in 2029 rather than fill in November.

Buy if the bay is empty now. The 19.9% certification rate is the argument against treating apprenticeship as recruitment, and 436 certificates a year in Ontario is the argument for taking retention of the licensed people you already have seriously.

Most shops need both, and the mistake is running only one.
